Mr. Speaker, last evening in dealing with this very important subject I said I was speaking in all humility because I realized the breadth and diversity of the problems we face when we discuss matters having to do with foreign relations. I listened attentively to the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who to a certain extent criticized the amount of money being voted for external affairs. Personally I have always been in favour of the strictest economy in all departmental activities, but in my view the total of some $9,000,000 being spent on external affairs is one of the finest investments this country could make.
The hon. member for Broadview, along with every other hon. member of this house and every citizen of this country, is to some extent responsible for the extension and expansion of the external affairs department; and I will amplify this statement. Up to the time of the South African war at the end of last century Canada and the United States were in a complacent mood, because in those days we realized, and had reason to believe, that we were protected by the British navy, while the Monroe doctrine was fully implemented as far as the great American nation was concerned. It is an historical fact, knowm now to everyone who wants to study history impartially, that the Monroe doctrine was capable of implementation purely and simply because of the wonderful shield and protection afforded by the British navy to all civilized' nations, and this applied most certainly to the American republic.
In the 1910's, for instance, who would have thought we were going to have a world war, in which every country would be directly interested and eventually participating? Geographically speaking Canada was supposed to stand

apart from any European conflict. We had then thrown aside any idea of participating in any imperialistic war. But the moment we heard that shot at Sarajevo, when the Austrian duke was killed for political reasons, even on this continent we realized that the world was smaller than we knew it in the nineteenth century. It was true that we had no fear from the north. We had no potential enemy there and were protected by nature, by the Arctic ocean and ice cap. It was also true that we had no fear from the south, because we thought and lived much the same as our American friends did. In those days many of us asked' ourselves why we should participate in a European conflict, and why we should not let the nations of Europe settle their own problems, by war if they wanted to do so. Undoubtedly that opinion was held even more strongly by our friends to the south. But it did not take us long to realize that we were part and parcel of the whole world, and that no longer could we consider keeping ourselves isolated from the rest of the nations, no matter how far away they are from our borders.
That is why Canada participated, rightly and gloriously, in the war of 1914-18. Eor many dreary, deadly months we hoped and prayed that the great nation to the south also would participate on the side of democracy and freedom. Eventually, after the Lusitania disaster, they realized that it was also their war. They knew their own shores were no longer immune; that if there was danger to England there was danger to France and the whole of Europe from the hordes of the Kaiser and of Austria; there was also danger to her own soil. They suddenly realized that they had to come into the conflict and stay until the bitter end so as to save democracy and freedom.
Then in 1939, after a period of peace which was all to short, again we realized that the world was growing smaller. National frontiers had disappeared owing to the great advances in physical science. We were all brothers together. It is true that we had to go through the humiliation of Munich; but perhaps that had to be because we were not realists. All the democracies were hoping and praying that we would not have another war such as we had from 1914 to 1918. But we know what happened in 1939; and to her great glory and honour once more Canada realized that she had to be in that battle for Christianity, freedom and democracy. As in 1914 we realized that even if it meant the tribulations of a horrible conflict, those barbaric hordes led by Hitler and Mussolini had to be confined within the borders of Europe
['Mr. Bradette.]
and detroyed there; that otherwise they would spread death and destruction throughout the continents of the world.
It took quite a while for our friends to the south to realize how serious was the situation, and again we must thank a kind Providence that in those troubled days the head of the great American republic was one of the greatest statesmen the world has ever known. He appreciated then the seriousness of the situation, though he was a pacifist like our Prime Minister, like the members of this parliament and every Canadian. We were praying and hoping for peace, but he knew the storm clouds which were hovering over Europe were bound to spread to every section of the world. Almost by himself, by his own courageous actions, he aroused American public opinion even before Pearl Harbor.
I have been told on good authority that in a discouraged moment Mr. Roosevelt confided to one of his best friends that though he had thrown everything he had into the battle, his great talent, his high office, his wonderful oratorical eloquence, he was afraid he was losing ground before American public opinion. But then came Pearl Harbor. It is true that prior to this Mr. Roosevelt and leading Americans of all parties in that great nation had heard appeals from Great Britain, which was almost alone for over a year, the only human rampart against the hordes of barbarism, paying the horrible cost in young lives and old lives and in destruction of indescribable magnitude. Mr. Roosevelt and the United States were told that Britain was fighting the barbarians in defence of democracy and freedom; but it was not enough. It took something like Pearl Harbor to make the American nation realize and to direct its policy accordingly, that though this occurred thousands of miles away it was an attack on the American nation, the same as if it had happened in the heart of New York, for instance. From that time on they have been fighting on our side, although their hearts were always with us, from the beginning of the conflict in 1939, through to the end.
That is why I say that it was not of our own choosing that we participated, but our way of life was in danger of destruction. I know that the contribution we made was a necessary one, although costly, and every citizen of this country has reason to be well pleased with our part, although dolorous in it.
As I said before, from the standpoint of geography it could be considered that we were not only pacifist but also isolationist. All that disappeared, because we suddenly realized

that every citizen in the world was to a large extent his brother's keeper. That principle has been evident throughout two wars, and it is being just as strongly pressed forward at the present time to emphasize our ideology. Because for every man, every woman and every child in this world, we pray and-wish for peace. In the back of our minds, however, and in our private and public deliberations, we cannot get away from the fact that there is a skeleton in the nation's closet, the skeleton of war. If it were possible to have a plebiscite today among all the citizens of the world they would vote one hundred per cent for peace. But there must be a diabolical genie that finds it possible periodically to develop a situation which tries the patience of individuals and of nations.
I maintain that through the united nations organization, to which we properly belong, and to which Canada has made a great contribution, we are fulfilling a high and constructive purpose. If the voice of Canada is listened to and respected through its spokesman, the right hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), to whose eloquence we listened yesterday, and if the ideals he has set forth prevail in that worldwide forum at Lake Success and at Flushing Meadows, we do not need to despair.
We shall have to guard ourselves in our own actions and pronouncements; but, at the same time, anyone who attended the meetings of the united nations last fall will say that the voice of Canada is highly respected and eagerly listened to. The reason for that is simple. In proportion to our population we have done more than any other nation of the world. And there is more than that to the reason why Canada is so highly respected in the forum of the United Nations. After giving of our lives and our resources through our courageous participation in the last two world conflicts, we do not ask for any territorial aggrandizement. We do not wish any additional territory in the Atlantic or the Pacific, nor do we want even any rectification of our own borders, which in some parts are anomalous. If we wanted to be selfish we could be; we could ask for some reward for what we have done in the two great wars, to try to rectify our borders. But we do not w'ant to do that, because we do not want to carry on agitation in respect of any question which might bring friction, when peace deliberations are our chief concern.
Some doubt was expressed yesterday as to the respect in which the Canadian delegation is held. Let me repeat that the voice of Canada is highly respected. There are in these precincts some who were delegates of 5849-221J
or advisers for Canada in the united nations organization. They knew that the best way to win the hearts and minds of the people they met was to say that they were Canadians. Immediately there was a sympathetic response; they spoke their minds to us, and left no doubt as to how much they greatly admired the wonderful things that this relatively small nation has accomplished.
These are reasons for great pride. I have seen with my own eyes many nations asking the advice of and a lead from Canada, because they respect our views, and1 they respect the action we have taken in our own history. I appreciate sincerely the action taken by the government last fall when I was appointed a delegate to the united nations organization in New York. I know, as chairman of the committee on external affairs, that there were many occasions in the course of our deliberations in that committee on which I was agreeably surprised by the knowledge shown by members of the committee. I have in mind the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and others-I have no time to give all their names-who were sent as delegates, as alternate delegates or advisers to San Francisco, to London and to New York. They gave every evidence of having taken a constructive part in those deliberations. I can say that those who were appointed as delegates or alternates left a fine impression as Canadians and as men who understood both national and international situations.
Last fall, with others, I happened to be a delegate from Canada. All parties were represented. I do not wish to give the names, but I can say sincerely that each participated to the best of his ability, and I take pleasure in paying them this tribute. They worked there as Canadians, realizing fully the seriousness of the problems they were facing.
It is no sinecure to be appointed a delegate, an alternate or an adviser in united nations activities. I know that those from the press gallery who attended the last session of the united nations were unanimous in their report as to the activities of the Canadian delegation. They all agreed that we had worked-not eight hours a day, because there was no question of union hours in those circumstances, but from twelve to fourteen hours every day. We did it diligently and willingly. I do not hesitate to repeat that the hon. member for Peel, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and all others who participated in previous meetings and deliberations made a fine impression on all who had the benefit of
Supply-External Affairs

listening to and meeting them, because I often had occasion to observe their fine accomplishments.
It was a new experience for me as a parliamentarian, and one I appreciated. That was the first time in many years I have had the great honour of being a member of parliament that it had been possible for me to mix with high officials of the civil service-high officials in a very important department. I know I gained much by my contact with those career men.
I do not need to mention names, because Canada has been most fortunate in her high officials in the civil service, and particularly in the foreign affairs branch. I could mention the names of Mr. Pearson and Mr. McNaughton, and many others who are making it their life's work to serve in that important department.
It was inevitable that as members of parliament, we were not always familiar with the methods of members of the civil service, but I believe if there was any light friction or any personal reaction the parliamentarians benefited by having been in contact with those high government officials. I have no doubt, too, that the benefit was reciprocal, and that the members of the service benefited by being in contact with men who had taken part in the hurly-burly of active politics, men who must face all conditions, from day to day, and from year to year, and must be prepared to meet public opinion. The contact between those two groups was bound to be beneficial in our deliberations and actions at the united nations meetings.
If an invitation is extended to any member of parliament to appear before the united nations in any capacity, I would urge him to accept it. He will know in advance that he will have to work, but he will enjoy it, because there is a feeling of accomplishment. And we can say that so far as our consideration of external affairs is concerned, the matter has been taken practically out of politics, and this is certainly a great credit to our parliament.
I want to compliment the administration for the fine move they made when they found it possible to have every section of the House of Commons and the Senate represented at the united nations. It is in that way that the government gels closer co-operation and has better work done.
I wish to make a brief reference to our connection with the United States. I may be prejudiced, but I love the United States; I love the Americans, and this attitude does not lessen my love for Canada. The United States is a big exuberant country possessing 
all the qualities and all the faults of a young, strong giant. Some of us would seem to be afraid of the size of the United States and the important place that it has been projected into. In the course of this debate reference has been made to two worlds, to two philosophies, Soviet Russia in the east and the United States of America on the American continent.
One colossus, Russia, was built up during the last seven centuries. That country carries on today the same imperialistic expansionist idea which was evident back in the ninth century and which has been her continuous policy. Europe and the rest of the world has often suffered from that expansionism. Today the United States is the second so-called world colossus. But she did not reach that stature of her own volition or with any idea of expansion. It was not done by her own work.
I think I showed at the beginning of my remarks that the United States, on account of her prosperity, her high standard of living, her strength, her wonderful natural resources, her climatic conditions, her isolation from Asia and Europe by two great expanses of water, never in her wildest dreams imagined that she would become the leading nation of the world. She was compelled to do so. I think this is an example of the ways of Providence as shown through history, as applied to individuals as well as to nations.
What would have happened in 1914-18 if there had been no United States? That democratic nation did not want to expand her territory. She was satiated as far as territory was concerned; but she answered the call of democracy which she knew was in danger in Europe. There is no doubt that she helped to a great extent to save European civilization, yes the whole world. She applied that principle just as forcibly, if not more forcibly, in 1939. She did not want to participate in a second war. Her people did not want a second war. Why should they want war? They were prosperous; within their own borders they had the highest standard of living of any nation in the world. They were a creditor nation; they were on friendly terms with everyone. They did not want to expand their territory. The territory which she might have annexed unjustly in the past she gave back. She gave those people their freedom. This house should realize that that great nation did not become powerful of her own volition. It was simply because there were compelling circumstances, and she

Supply-External Affairs
realized the role she had to play at the cost of great sacrifices, in defending civilization and freedom.
Is it fair to make a comparison between the United States ideology and Russian Soviet ideology? Can a favourable comparison be made between communism and progressive capitalism? Such comparisons are not right, yet they are made time and again in this House of Commons. As I said a moment ago, the United States has all the exuberance of a fine, powerful youth. She knows her strength; she knows her ability to produce, but she is also magnanimous. I listened attentively last night to the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He said that in the last war we repeated practically the same errors that we had made in the previous war, that there had been an expansion of territory, the annexation of new population and the use of slave labour in the mines and forests of the victorious nations. Surely that would not apply to the United States.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar seems to deplore the fact that the United States wants to have defensive outposts on the Pacific ocean. I for one am in favour of such outposts. The United States does not want them for purposes of aggrandizement. T ask hon. members to think of the situation of Australia and New Zealand during the last war. A large number of the courageous sons of those countries were fighting in North Africa when the attack on Pearl Harbor occurred. After Pparl Harbor their countries were in deadly danger. In those horrible hours after the Philippines were crushed, over two-thirds of the United States navy was destroyed. General MacArthur had to leave the Philippines as a vanquished general, his magnificent armed forces completely destroyed. He went to Australia, and there he was received with open arms. The people in Australia were a little impatient. They wanted to know what was going to happen when their sons were fighting in North Africa and their own shores were in deadly danger. These outposts are needed. If I have any voice in advising my government I hope that we never find it possible to criticize them.
What do they mean? They mean that there is a safeguard for the civilized world, for all free-loving people, for all free-loving nations the same as the British navy to a large extent was a safeguard for the peace-loving nations of the world. This is not the time and place to propound any theories about the great British empire which is not
disintegrating but is merely growing into the British commonwealth of nations.
1 repeat that these outposts are not for United States aggrandizement; they are for the safety of the whole world. They are not a threat to any nation that wants to remain peaceful. There was no idea o{ threat in the outpost of Pearl Harbor. When the attack on Pearl Harbor took place the Japanese ambassador, who was supposed to be talking peace to the United States government, must have known that the attack had been planned by the military caste in Japan. We do not want a repetition of that situation. Prevention is better than cure.
Supposing the United States had had no outpost at Pearl Harbor? Supposing that that horrible holocaust had occurred in San Francisco harbour? It might have proved a deadly blow to the United States. With the situation that we must of necessity face in the world today we must have these outposts. They are not for purposes of war; they are merely to tell the nations of the world that they are more than United States outposts, that they are world outposts which will stand guard for all nations which desire peace and freedom. Any nation that believes in peace will not have to worry. The navy, the marines, the army and the air force will be there for one purpose only, the maintenance of the peace of the world. The United States are telling all the peaceful nations to call on them if anyone dares to attack them unjustly, and the United States will answer that call immediately and effectively. That is my way of thinking.

Mr. Speaker. I am sure that all members of the house will join with the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) in the fine words with which he closed his speech.
I am glad that my first word this afternoon is to congratulate the minister of external affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) on his comprehensive and constructive statement on our country's position in world affairs. I think it must be a source of considerable satisfaction to him that the statement he made yesterday has received so much support in this chamber that there is very little left to be said by way of criticism.
If I understand the government's policy as the minister stated it yesterday, and I believe I do, it is, stated briefly, to use the united

Supply-External Affairs
nations as the instrument for maintaining world security and advancing world welfare. However, the minister went further, and here I agree with him. If the united nations does not provide us with the security we seek, then we shall co-operate with other democratic nations to provide that security for us and for them. In my opinion that is a realistic policy; it is a policy with which I agree and with which I think every member of this group agrees. As a matter of fact I suppose it is forced on us by world events, by the shortcomings of the united nations.
It was my good fortune to attend the meetings of the general assembly of the united nations last fall. I say it was my good fortune, although the meeting itself was not very inspiring; but it did give me the opportunity of seeing the organization at work and to meet and hear and see world personalities in action. I am sorry that more members of parliament are not able to attend those meetings. As the hon. member for Cochrane said on his own behalf during the course of his speech, I wish to thank the government for giving me that opportunity and to say how much I appreciated working with the delegation and the members of the external affairs staff.
I believe 'the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who attended the general assembly as one of the 'parliamentary advisers, as I was, said that his advice was not accepted. I do not know whether mine was accepted or not, but I can say that I had every opportunity of giving it, and when I did not do so on any question that came up I was invariably asked for my opinion. No one could wish for anything more than that.
We all agree that the united nations has fallen far short of the hopes that we had for it when the charter was signed in 1945. That being so I think this afternoon I shall try to show what in my opinion is the reason for its failure. I hope I shall not be too critical, buit what I shall say is what has been impressed upon me, not only by (my attendance at the general assembly last fall but by my observation of international events since the end of world war II.
The charter of the united nations is its constitution. The signatories to that charter, if they signed it sincerely, accepted certain principles which would govern their conduct as members of the united nations. Probably the principles I am going to state would not be acceptable to everyone, but they appear to me to be the principles on which the organization of the united nations is based. The first principle is that -nations with different political and economic systems can co-operate for certain purposes. Even if those
purposes are limited, those signing the charter felt there could be co-operation; otherwise there was no point in signing it. The second principle is that no nation should interfere with the internal affairs of another -nation, and the third, that membership in the united nations meant the acceptance of compromise in the settlement of international disputes.
As I said, from my observations at the general assembly last fall, I became convinced that these principles, at least for certain members of the united nations, no -longer operate. There is now definitely a division in the united nations on political and economic lines. The Soviet bloc rejects those principles which democratic nations consider the foundation stone of their very existence; while the democratic countries reject those principles on which authoritarian states are based. It is from these fundamental, and I think irreconcilable, differences that conflicts in the united nations stem.
As it appeared to me at the general assembly, the delegates of the Soviet union made no attempt whatsoever to minimize differences or to find grounds for co-operation. Every effort was taken to emphasize differences and to prevent agreement, to use the united nations, as Mr. Vishinsky said in one of his speeches, as a propaganda forum. So long as that spirit exists on one side, the united nations, however useful it may be, will not do for the people of the world what we hoped it would do when it was formed.
On the other hand, I am convinced that the other nations, particularly the democratic countries, are anxious to co-operate with the Soviet union. There was always great joy when the Soviet delegates gave the slightest indication that there could be co-operation. If anyone thinks that the statement I have just made with reference to the attitude of the Soviet union is too sweeping I would draw attention to the excessive use of the veto by that nation in the security council, and to the boycott of general assembly decisions with which they did not agree. The decisions with which they did agree were never particularly important.
But there is a further indication of the unwillingness of the Soviet union to work with other nations. There are associated or affiliated with the united nations certain specialized agencies. I believe there are eleven of these altogether. As far as I can learn the Soviet union has representation on only four, on the world health organization, and on the international trade organization-and I believe that is only partial, being limited to the preparatory committee. They also have representation on the universal postal union and
Supply-External Affairs

on the international telecommunication union. The Soviet, union has no representatives on the international labour organization or on the food and agriculture organization, two organizations which are very important, if for no other reason, so far as the international labour organization is concerned, than that it brings together employers and employees from all parts of the world to discuss questions which are of importance to industrial workers. The food and agriculture organization is of the utmost importance today if we are to have international co-operation in increasing the food supply of the world. The Soviet union has no representation on UNESCO, on the international civil aviation organization, on the international bank, on the international monetary fund, or, as far as I know, on the international refugee organization.
I have mentioned this matter because these specialized agencies, along with the principal organs of the united nations, are the means by which the principles of the united nations charter can be made effective in the lives of the peoples of the world; and I would give it as my opinion that it is most important that all countries should be represented on them. This abstaining from membership in these agencies can only mean that the Soviet union does not believe in co-operation among the peoples of the world. As I said before, until there is a change in that attitude the united nations organization will not be the force in world affairs that we had hoped it would be.
As long as there is any hope, however, that the united nations organization can be of use, we must do everything possible to keep it in existence, even if we are disappointed with its progress. It is an inspiring ideal, and some day it may work. I agree with the hon. member for Cochrane that even if it only provides a forum for the discussion of world problems it is serving a useful purpose. If such is the case I hope the government will give it every support, and I am sure they will.
I come now to the other part of the government's policy, that if we cannot have all the nations of the world in one organization, we must do what sensible people always do when they cannot have all they want, namely, do the next best thing. The next best thing in this case, I think, is the announcement made by the Secretary of State for Externa! Affairs of co-operation with the democratic countries of western Europe. Here I should like to express publicly my own appreciation of the action of the United States in providing the funds for the European recovery program. This is economic aid given by one country to other countries on a scale never

before dreamed of. As I said, I wish to express my own appreciation of that generosity.
The motives of the United States in making this aid available have been questioned. But whatever the motives, can anyone in his senses object to feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and putting into the hands of the war-tortured people of Europe the means by which they can rebuild their industries and restore their dignity? I cannot understand, on the part of anyone who believes in human welfare, objection to a program of that kind. It is unfortunate and even deplorable that Soviet Russia did not allow the countries of eastern Europe to participate in this recovery program. But I hope that the benefits of the European recovery program will seep into eastern Europe, as I am convinced they will, and that these countries will benefit from the operations of the program. It would have been much more pleasant and much better for the people of the world if this program had been accepted in all the countries of Europe on the basis on which it was offered.
A great deal has been said during the session, and particularly yesterday, about the dangers of communism and the appeal it had to many people in various parts of the world. I think we should try to understand why it is that people will accept the solution of communist revolution for their problems. I feel that sometimes in this house, because of our own comfortable position, we do not appreciate the outlook of millions of people in other lands who have never known anything but hunger and privation. 'Let us just remember that in almost all countries up to the present, with perhaps the exception of the North American countries, only a small group at the top were ever economically secure, and consequently politically secure; because a person who is not economically secure cannot be either politically secure or politically free. For the great masses of people in all countries the important thing in their lives is bread. Hungry people are always thinking of things to eat. Until we are able to convince them that democracy will give them not only the opportunity to vote but also the opportunity to eat, they will fall for slogans such as "the land for the peasants" and "the factories for the workers," and will always, in my opinion, lose out as well. That is what we must do today. We must not only give the people political freedom and political democracy; we must make sure that with our joint co-operation they will also have bread.

Both the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the hon. member for Stanstead referred to the political changes which have come about in our international relations during the last three or four decades. These changes have been great, so great indeed that foreign relations are no longer the exclusive concern of foreign ministers and their diplomatic staffs. Today our international affairs reach down to the farmer on the land, the miner in the mine and the industrial worker in the factory. That is so because of the importance of production in our international affairs. In a word, international relations today are no longer a question of the manoeuvring by politicians and diplomats to have their country come out on the long end of international deals. International relations are becoming more and more a matter of co-operation in the- improving of human welfare and human security.
We in Canada therefore will have to see to it that our farmers understand the part their production plays in maintaining world peace. The miners of Great Britain will have to understand the part they play in providing coal for Europe's needs; and workers in the factories all over the world must be shown that they, too, are important in maintaining peace in this new world in which we find ourselves.
Last winter one of the Ottawa newspapers ran a series of articles condensing the memoirs of Mr. Cordell Hull. I was interested to note what Mr. Hull had to say about his fight for freer trade and the lowering of tariff barriers by the United States, and what he felt was the part played by economic factors in our relations with other countries. I should like to read briefly from one of those articles. He said:
Over and -above the economic side of our foreign policy, but closely tied in with it, I believed, hung the political side. To me it seemed virtually impossible to develop friendly relations with other nations in the political sphere as long as we provoked' their animosity in the economic sphere. How could we promote peace with them while waging war on them commercially? When I came into the state department I found in the department files no fewer than thirty-four formal and emphatic diplomatic protests presented by as many nations following the passage of the Smoot-Hawley high tariff act. Nor had their protests been confined to words. Goaded by what they regarded as almost an embargo keeping out their exports to the United' States, they retaliated in kind.
If we are to have peace in the world we should remember certain things today. The industrial productive potential of the world is enormous, indeed so enormous that, given
a few years of peace, it will be more than sufficient to meet the needs of a world at peace. The march goes on, not alone in the fields of Europe and Asia but in the minds of men all over the world. The march ultimately can be arrested only when we demonstrate to them that behind this temporary face of force-and I repeat, this temporary face of force-lie the benevolent, kindly heart and hand of a democratic people which genuinely desires to see a square deal for all; and when we say "all" we mean exactly what we say.
That way, Mr. Speaker, lies progress. That way lies prosperity. That way lies security. That way lies peace.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house are particularly happy because of the strong stand taken in this chamber yesterday afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) against communism and communist activities throughout the world. We were also pleased to see the leaders and spokesmen of the opposition parties throw their spontaneous support behind the minister's statement of government policy with respect to

Sup-ply-External Affairs
foreign affairs, and more especially in regard to the official announcement of Canadian support for the collective security pact among the western democracies within the framework of the united nations. The participation in this debate of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was also a valuable contribution; and of course I am perfectly satisfied that no part of his address was intentionally designed to be used as propaganda in the coming Ontario election.
I do not wish to take much of the time of this house in participating in this important debate. I am far from pretending to be an expert in these complicated matters of international relations; nevertheless I should be quite satisfied with myself if I could succeed in expressing a few ideas representative of some of the points of view of the man on the street, who, in the last analysis, is the one who pays the price for war and the one who is called upon to pay the price for peace.
We learn from history that from time immemorial generations of men of different racial origins in all countries of the world have sought methods of preserving peace. For thousands of years nations have brought their wars to an end by the signing of treaties designed by men with the object of establishing permanent if not perpetual peace. Yet up to our time war has never been abolished as a means of settling international disputes and differences between nations. We participated in the first world war on the assumption that afterwards the world was to enjoy an unlimited period of peace. Tire first world war did not achieve the objective of establishing a lasting peace. During the greatest struggle of all time, world war II, which was imposed upon the free democracies of the world, we were told repeatedly that this time everything would be settled forever. It did not settle anything. At least in 1918, at the close of the first world war, the world seemed ready for peace. Today we find such a state of confusion in international relations that one must reach the conclusion that the nations of the world seem ready neither for war nor for peace.
From the point of view of a multitude of Canadians, lasting peace seems further away at this moment than at any time since the close of hostilities; and a great many think it is beyond our grasp. We live in an atmosphere of instability, insincerity and insecurity. Obviously the fault lies somewhere. But it is no contribution to the solution of this crucial problem merely to say that the fault lies with the other power, with the other country,
and let ourselves drift into the unknown without attempting to do something to remedy the situation.
Owing to its strategic position and its economic importance, our country of Canada can play a greater part in the establishment of lasting peace, and has as much responsibility, as, if not more, for pursuing that objective and aim, than most countries of the world. We stand here in the centre of a great struggle. In one way we are the shock absorbers of a gigantic clash between two ideologies, and perhaps I might add, between two shapes of imperialism. There is a war, a cold war, now being fought on ideological grounds. Let us admit to ourselves that the two great goals at the opposite ends of those grounds are imperialism. They belong to the U.S.S.R. team, we belong to the British-American team.
There are some who advocate the suppression of communism by waging another world war. This suggestion finds scores of sympathizers, even in the province of Quebec. I feel that this is entirely wrong, and for various reasons which seem obvious, one of the reasons being that no philosophy has ever been seized and destroyed by war. One cannot destroy a philosophy; one cannot destroy a single idea in this world by the use of bullets; and it will never be done even by the contribution of the frightful power of atomic bombs.
The only possible cure for the discontent found amongst people living under our system of democracy, here in Canada or outside in the world, is to make this democratic way of life work so well that its superiority cannot be challenged, either here in Canada or in any other democratic nation. The only way an idea can be killed is to bring along a better idea.
We have here in Canada political freedom and an immense heritage of wealth. Let us first secure for our country as a whole, and for the people living within the boundaries of this nation, a full measure of economic freedom, as well as a full measure of social security. Second, let us contribute our full share, in order to spread, through our moral and material assistance, this priceless economic freedom and social security to the other nations of the world, which are in such need of our Christian, charitable help, in this crucial period of the history of mankind.
We have paid a terrible price through our participation in two great world wars. We have just paid the price for a most devastating total war. That should be enough. Unless we are ready to take the inconceivable risk of
Supply-External Affairs

diving blindly into a third world war, which could be a final catastrophe engulfing the whole world, with frightening consequences, let us now be prepared to pay the price for a total peace.
Let us have the courage to tell that story to our constituents, to our own people; and let us have enough brains to talk less about the possibility of participating in a third world war, as a means of destroying communism and restoring a Christian order of charity and justice throughout the world.
Obviously, between the ideologies of Soviet Russia and those of the United States and of the British commonwealth, there is just as great a gulf as existed in 1939 between the allied nations and Hitler's Germany.
But until all countries learn that each nation must be allowed to have, without outside pressure, the ideology it likes best, there can be only very much restricted common ground for the discussion and solution of other problems. We fear that the communist states have not yet learned this; and that is precisely what makes the present position of the world so tragic.
Owing to these exceptionally sad circumstances, and in order to help avoiding a third world war and to promote an enduring peace, we must at all costs, along with the other peace-loving free democracies of the world, be united behind policies designed to promote our own common interest and to safeguard their security as well as our own.
Furthermore, in the councils of the nations we must throw all our weight behind the idea that no peace can be lasting, unless it is established on the natural rights of all countries of the world to equal economic opportunity, whether that country be France, China, Italy, Spain or even Germany.
So long as any one nation, whether it be the United States or Russia, possesses a monopoly over natural resources or raw materials which are needed by all nations, there can be no sound basis for a world order based on justice and on peace. So as Canadians let us start out this peace planning properly, by first establishing, in as great measure as we can, economic freedom and social security for the benefit of our own people, and, second, by contributing our share to bring about the fullest collaboration between all peace-loving free nations of the world. Let us do this to help toward the establishment of equality of trade conditions among all countries, in order to improve the standard of living conditions, national and individual economic advancement and social justice, for all people of all nations.

Another world war, fought with atomic power and modern war equipment, can only mean almost entire destruction of our present civilization. That is the threat which lies in front of each one of us, unless we are ready to pay the price for total peace.
Our democratic Christian philosophy teaches us that man is not made for war, whether it be war between nations or war between classes. It further teaches us, not that war is inevitable, but rather that peace is inevitable if we would only recognize that all men are brothers, and that God is their Father.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great attention to the speeches which have been made in this debate, and first I should like to congratulate all those who have spoken before me. I give them credit for their sincerity and I hope they will credit me with a like sincerity. The other day I listened to a broadcast from Lake Success and the speaker said that the time had come for plain speaking. I intend1 to speak plainly this afternoon.
For the purposes of this debate I shall recognize no political party as such, not even my own. For me there are only two kinds of people to be considered when dealing with external affairs. There are those whose first loyalty is to Canada, a sovereign state within the sovereign nations of the British commonwealth, and there are those whose loyalty is to something outside Canada and the British commonwealth. I do not care what they call it, but anyway it is a loyalty which is given to something outside Canada and outside the British commonwealth of nations. Whether these internationalists like it or not, all communists and all pink fellow travellers are among those who give their loyalty to something wider than the country in which they happen to live. I do not say that all internationalists are communists, but I do say that all communists are internationalists. It seems to me that the education of those internationalists who are not communists has exceeded the scope of their intelligence.
The real threat of communism to this country and to all other countries at the present time does not come directly from Russia, nor does it come from outside the country or from the members of the communist party within the country. It is not the Tim Bucks who constitute the threat to this country. Although I disagree violently with their ideas, I have some measure of respect for those .men because at least they have the honesty to say what they are and what they stand for. The real threat and danger to Canada and to those other countries which still preserve their freedom

Supply-External Affairs
come from those people who talk freedom when they are secretly plotting to bring about the tyranny of communism.
Reference was made the other day by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) to an editorial which had appeared in a Vancouver paper, and I believe also in a Winnipeg paper. Along with me the editor referred also to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). Of course the editor brought me into it as usual as having indulged in anti-Semitic diatribes. This is the communist smear and it is always used by them. To my knowledge the hon. member for Macleod has never so much as referred either to Jews or even to the Zionists, and yet as soon as he names these fellow travellers he is smeared with anti-Semitism in the press.
The press has marked my activities ever since the occasion in this house six years ago when I denounced a certain newspaperman who had publicly advocated the surrender of the sovereignty of this country to something wider than Canada and wider than the British commonwealth of nations. From that day to this, everything that I have said has been twisted or ignored by a large part of our press.
Communism has been spread internationally by the secret agreements which were made during the war and since the war, and I refer to Yalta, Teheran and Potsdam. Through those agreements which were secretly arrived at, the greater part of eastern Europe was delivered into the hands of the communists. Greece and China were partly betrayed and would have been fully betrayed had it not been that the authorities awakened to the danger of the communist threat.
I remember defending in this house the British policy in Greece when Great Britain stepped in there to stop the communist revolution. At once I was assailed as a fascist andl the British were condemned for their imperialism and attempting to restore discredited monarchs and reactionary governments. I said I would not mention any political party, but that was the statement made by the hon. member for Rose town-Bi ggar (Mr. Coldwell). I presume he spoke for his party, but anyway that was the line he took.
Then there was the betrayal of Mihailovich. He was sold down the river and his country was delivered into the hands of Tito. I stood in this house alone when I defended Mihailovich, an honourable man who had stood by us all through the war. But under political pressure he was turned aside and Tito was adopted for purposes of allied; support.
An extraordinary incident came to light recently through the publication of the memoirs of Mr. Cordell Hull, former secretary of state of the United States. He tells us in his diary what took place in September, 1944, at the Quebec conference:
I said bluntly to the President that Mor-genthau's plan-
It was the Morgenthau plan that was
adopted at Quebec.
-was out of all reason and that no experts or officials of our government had had anything to do with its preparation. Morgenthau's plan, I added, would wipe out everything in Germany, except land, and the Germans would have to live on the land. This meant that only 60 per cent of the German people could live on German land and the other 40 per cent would die.
I concluded that I was satisfied that the British at Quebec had joined in on this extreme starvation plan in order to get Morgenthau's help in obtaining the six and a half billion dollar credit proposed by the secretary of the treasury.
That is the statement of the former secretary of state of the United States, and in this connection may I refer to the remarks of the leader of this group in the house last night when he called attention to the power of international finance? Here is one example of it. In plain English, in order to get the loan the British had to sign on the dotted line. I called attention to that in this house in August, 1946. I knew nothing, of course, of the secret agreement reached at Quebec, but I had this to say of the policy that was becoming evident in Europe:
Mussolini and Hitler are dead, and the war in Europe ended over a year ago. But the people of Europe are more hungry and more miserable than they were during the war. What is the reason? Famine can result from a lack of harvest or of transport; it can be imposed deliberately for political purposes. For political reasons German fertilizer plants which formerly supplied European farmers have been destroyed. No locomotives can he built in Germany until 1950. Stalin took the only food surplus area in Germany and now, as the socialist Daily Worker says, food is an international political weapon.
When we blame conditions in Europe for the spread of communism let us remember that many of those conditions were deliberately and designedly brought about to spread communism wherever possible. That is one instance that bears out what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said last night in reference to international finance.
I now want to say a few words about Palestine. First of all, I should like to pay a tribute to those British soldiers and policemen and civil administrators in Palestine
Supply-External Affairs

who, through all these years, have borne the brunt of savagery and gangsterism, many of them unarmed but shot in the back, even hanged and then turned into booby traps. That has been their lot, and their reward has been to be smeared as brutal, even as brutal as the Germans. I have witnessed that on more than one visit to the United States. I have seen and heard anti-British propaganda there which would make any Briton's blood boil. Zionists have even sent their agents to this country to deliver addresses in Canadian cities where they have made the most disparaging statements about the behaviour of the British in Palestine. In my opinion no soldiers and no policemen ever acted in a better or in a more humane way than the British have done in Palestine, and I want to make that clear.
I have not time to go into the Palestine question except as it bears on the peace of the world. As hon. members know, I have been opposed to political zionism almost since I have been a member of this house, and I have never hesitated to state my opposition to it and the reasons for doing so.
Speaking in Montreal in July, 1946, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) said:
"Many people think the British Labour party is allied with the C.C.F. party in Canada, but that is not so. There may be some similarity as to certain points, but the C.C.F. could never ally itself with a government that had broken a promise such as that to the Jews in Palestine." Politics of this sort, he said, were not within the spirit of socialism.
I deny that the British have broken any promise to the Jews in Palestine or anywhere else. The Jews have had better treatment irom the British than from any other people. The hon. member for Winnipeg North went on to urge the immediate entrance of 100,000 Jews into Palestine, and the newspaper report says:
Mr. Stewart ridiculed the idea that such immigration would lead to an Arab revolt.
Now see the tragic consequences of that policy; but when I pointed out in this House of Commons and elsewhere the inevitable consequences of Zionist policy I was immediately attacked by the press, by the C.B.C. and everywhere else as anti-Semitic.
I should mention a letter which I received in 1945 from the president of the Canadian Zionist League, in which he said:
I do not think Arab threats directed at Great Britain, the United States and other members of the united nations organization should be taken too seriously. They are a

species of blackmail from a primitive people by which they have profited in gold and various concessions in the past. Threats of violence have been the Arabs' most profitable stock in trade. How much longer are the great powers going to appease them? There is no doubt that a policy on Palestine agreed upon by the United States, Great Britain, and the other united nations will be one to which the Arabs will be forced to adjust themselves.
Force, not justice! What is the consequence of attempting to force a decision which itself was arrived at under pressure? The world is now faced with another world war, because war has started and, like a fire in a forest country, who is to say when and how it can be put out?
The British having withdrawn and having refused to participate in any program that is not accepted by both the Jews and the Arabs, and having refused to take part in any solution which needs the use of force, and the United States, for reasons of its own security and for reasons of preserving the peace of the world, having turned its back on partition, the Zionists turned their denunciation on the United States government. Here is a statement from the New York Post dated February 25, in which Rabbi Baruch Koi'ff had the following to say of the present United States government.:
This generation will have to answer to the generation that will inherit the mess of chicanery, the diabolical treachery, with which we govern our allies and friends, and constantly undermine the noblest of traditions which made America the land of the free. I cannot but look upon the shameless cycle of deceit as pure and simple anti-Semitism-no oil, no gold, no imperialism, but plain everyday anti-Semitism, incorporated in the hearts and minds of those who govern free America in 1948. This type of anti-Semitism, wrhich is today wrecking the lives of wretched souls-survivors of Auschnitz and Dachau-is even more dangerous than the venom of Hitler, because this form of antiSemitism is wrapped in the stars and stripes of free America, camouflaged in the words of Austin: "The council's action ... is directed to keeping the peace and not to enforcing partition."
Again in the New York Post the following editorial appears which refers to President Truman as trying to kill the united nations, and reads as follow's:
The President has no mandate to kill the united nations, however convenient this method of appeasing Arabia and Great Britain may seem to the men of power who are heedless of honour.
The United States government is now indicted as anti-Semitic because it puts the interests of world peace before those of the political Zionists.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with respect to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) a week ago tonight. At the outset I must say I was amazed that the hon. member should have taken advantage of the opportunity to speak to this amendment for twenty minutes and then call on Your Honour to rule it out of order. However, he chose that course and indicated, at page 3282 of Hansard for last Friday, that in his view there were two objections to the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough).
In the first instance, on the page to which I have referred, the hon. member quoted from citation 769 of Beauchesne, third edition, which indicates some difference between public and private bills, and said that, in the light of this citation, the amendment was meaningless. His whole case as far as that point is concerned was based upon the alleged difference between public and private bills; and on that basis he contended that we should not be amending the bill or opposing second reading, because it was only a conditional approval.
The second point raised by the hon. member is also indicated on page 3282 of

Hansard, where he said that the amendment now before the house was meaningless because-
... it would mean that we amend the Companies Act in a private bill.
That was an interesting comment for the hon. member to make, to say the amendment was meaningless and then turn around and give its meaning. However I wish to deal with the two points the hon. member raised.
The first point was that there is a difference between a public and private bill which makes an amendment of this nature, in his view, out of order. The hon. member referred to but did not quote citation 769. The part he referred to reads:
There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
That is the part of the citation which supports the position taken by the hon. member for Outremont. I would point out that he might have read a bit from another citation, 740, which says in part:
The house, in reading a private bill for the second time, decides that the matter involved is one which may be looked into by the committee.
In the same way citation 770, if you read only part of it, seems to support his position; for it says:
The house does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill, the house is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it is afterwards referred finds those allegations proved.
I admit that not only the citation from which the hon. member quoted but these other two citations, if read in part, seem to support his contention that there is something rather harmless about giving second reading to a private bill. His whole point, as I say, is that it is different from giving second reading to a public bill. But-and this is something one has always to watch-the hon. gentleman did not give the whole of citation 769.
I did not give any of it.
