Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable-
And that holds in this case.
-the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
Now note the next sentence, which states that the second reading of a private bill-
... is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
I submit that this indicates that when a bill is exceptional this is the time we have to oppose its principle. Similarly, if I go back to citation 740, part of which I read a moment ago, we find that the concluding sentence states:
It is only in case that an exceptional principle is enunciated that the second reading is refused.
Similarly in citation 770, if you read the last sentence:
It is usual, therefore, to allow a second reading, except where the bill enunciates some principle which the house is not prepared to affirm.
As those who have followed this discussion will readily recognize, we have felt that because it asks for such a large increase in authorized capitalization, this bill is calling upon the house to approve the enunciation of an exceptional principle. Therefore we feel perfectly in order in regarding this stage of this private bill as highly significant. I would go farther and point out other citations which raise a question about the propriety of this being a private bill at all. Citation 744 states:
The boundary line between private and public bills is narrow and has varied at different times. The house has refused to give a private bill a second reading on the ground that it Bhould have been introduced as a public bill.
And in citation 745:
Private bills frequently affect the general or public interests qf particular localities; and in some cases, from the extent to which such interests are affected, measures proposed as private bills have been declared unfit for private legislation and the parties have been required to proceed by public bill.
I submit that there is good ground not only for arguing against the position taken by the hon. member for Outremont that to give second reading to this bill is a harmless proposition, but actually that it enunciates
a principle so staggering, and it invades a field so close to the public field, that not only have we the right to do everything we can to defeat the bill at this stage, but we also have the right to question its propriety as a private bill at all.
With respect to the other point raised by the hon. member for Outremont, namely, that the amendment now before the house is meaningless, but with the meaning that it would be a case of amending the Companies Act by an amendment to a private bill, may I call Your Honour's attention to citation 657 in Beauchesne, third edition.
This is the basic citation which has to do with an amendment of this type to the second reading of a bill. In my view there is something important at stake here. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has just read this citation-at least he read the same words; whether he took it from the same place or not, I cannot say-so I shall not take time to repeat it. However it is there quite clearly, in the words the hon. member for Broadview quoted, that it is competent on second reading for a member to move as an amendment a resolution declaratory of some principle relating to the whole matter then before the house. It is not in order on second reading to move an amendment to the bill itself. It is not in order to move an amendment that is merely a direct negative. It is not in order to attach conditions to second reading. But it is in order, as I say, to move an amendment which expresses some principle related to the circumstances connected with the introduction of the bill.
That is precisely what the amendment does. Without referring to a specific section, the amendment notes that there is a question as to the amount of increased capital requested. The amendment therefore expresses, as a general statement of opinion, that no company ought to ask parliament for an increase in authorized capital in excess of 100 per cent. This bill happens to ask for an increase to the extent of 233 per cent.
The citation from Beauchesne, which the hon. member for Broadview quoted a few moments ago, is to be found at page 390 of May, thirteenth edition. After stating the general right of private members on second reading to move this type of amendment, May gives a considerable dissertation which leads up to this interesting paragraph, which answers the hon. member's point when he states that, to pass this amendment, would be to amend the Companies Act through the process of amending a private bill.
Bell Telephone Company

I suggest that it is important for hon. members to take note of {his paragraph, because questions are frequently being raised about this kind of amendment to second reading. I quote the following from page 392 of May, thirteenth edition:
It must be borne in mind, however, that the resolution if agreed to-
That is an amendment such as the one now before the house.
-does not arrest the progress of the bill, the second reading of which may be moved on another occasion. The effect of such an amendment is merely to supersede the question for now reading the bill a second time;-
The -word "now" is in italics. It continues: -and the bill is left in the same position as if the question for now reading the bill a second time had been simply negatived or superseded by the previous question. The house refuses, on that particular day, to read the bill a second time, and gives its reasons for such refusal: but the bill is not otherwise disposed of. Such being the technical effect of a resolution, so carried, it need scarcely be said that its moral and political results-
And those are the only kinds of results this amendment can have.
[DOT]-vary according to the character and importance of the resolution itself, the support it has received, and the means there may be of meeting it, in the further progress of the bill.
Then May goes on to give, from experience in the United Kingdom, cases where amendments of this kind have been before the house. Sometimes they have passed and sometimes they have been defeated. In particular he indicates that, when those amendments have passed, at times it has had the effect of defeating the government, and sometimes it has had almost no effect at all. But in all cases May makes it quite clear that the effect of this kind of amendment is purely moral and political. It does not have any operative effect. It does not amend the Companies Act at all. That suggestion is away off the mark.
Actually, as I say, it merely states the opinion of the house that this should not be done; and even if our amendment were carried-and I hope the house will support the principle enunciated in it-it still is competent for the hon. member for Outremont himself to rise in his place and to move that the bill be read a second time at some other date that he might fix.
I will call his attention, without taking time to read the citation, to Beauchesne, third edition, citation 663, and citation 710 from the same edition. The first has to do with second reading and the other with third reading. Those citations indicate that the defeat of the motion for second reading, whether it be a

vote on the motion itself or a vote on an amendment thereto, is not fatal to the bill. It is still in order for the member sponsoring the bill to rise in his place and to move that it be read a second or a third time at a stated sitting of the house.
And so the argument the hon. member puts forth to the effect that this amendment would have the effect of amending the Companies Act by amending a private bill falls to the ground. We have in this amendment, in the terms May has indicated, an attempt to do something which is a private member's right, namely to declare our reasons for opposing the progress of the bill.
I contend that the point which has been raised is a most important one, and relates not only to the bill before us tonight, but to members' rights generally with respect to second reading. I hope Your Honour will see fit to rule that the amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have listened attentively to what hon. members have said, and I wish to compliment them on presenting their case so clearly. I am, however, faced with certain difficulties.
In the first place, let me say that the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this is the time to accept or reject the principle of the bill, is quite in order. I agree with him in that.
But the question on which I must give a ruling is whether or not the amendment is in order. In that connection I would refer hon. members to Beauchesne, third edition, citation 771, where Mr. J. W. Lowther, who was chairman of committees of ways and means of the British House of Commons, made a statement with respect to private bills. This is what he said:
The rule which the house had generally followed and, he thought, very wisely, had been to allow the second reading of private bills to go through unless any strikingly new principle happened to be enunciated therein, and in such cases the house must pause before it accepts the principle.
At the present time I cannot see that any strikingly new principle is enunciated in this bill. I have no doubt other bills have been presented to the house in which capital has been greatly increased.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the fact that on second reading of a private bill the principle was affirmed, and as I have already stated I have no quarrel with that. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre added that if the

Bell Telephone Company
amendment carried, the bill could be introduced again immediately and be considered this session. I doubt, assuming he is right, if that is practicable at this late stage in the session. Certainly, if the bill had been deferred for three or six months or if it had been rejected, a new bill for the same object could not be presented at this session; reference Beauchesne, third edition, citation 773; for all practical purposes this bill could not be presented at this session. I refer hon. members to Beauchesne, third edition, citation 773. If this amendment carried the result would be to defer this bill at least until another session, which I say would be contrary to the opinion expressed by Mr. Lowther, which I quoted when I read from citation 771.
There is another difficulty with which I am faced, whether in connection with a private bill a general principle should be enunciated which would affect all bills. If the principle which is questioned at this time affected only this bill I do not think I would have difficulty in coming to a conclusion, but the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough) is in the following words:
That Bill No. 8 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house no company-
I emphasize the word "no".
-should ask parliament for an increase in authorized capital in excess of one hundred per cent.
This principle, if approved by this house, would affect all private bills. I would refer hon. members to the words used by the hon. member for Assiniboia when he moved his amendment, and I quote from page 3058 of Hansard:
I do not refer now particularly-
Note the word "particularly."
[DOT]-to this bill, but I say that as a principle we in the House of Commons should give expression to the idea that no company at any time should be granted a capitalization 100 per cent over and above its present capitalization.
I think hon. members will realize from that how far-reaching this amendment would be if it were allowed. May I also refer hon. members to citation 769 in Beauchesne, third edition, the effect of which has been referred to by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is stated there that on the second reading of a private bill the house affirms the principle of the bill. It has been intimated that there is very little difference, if any, between accepting the principle of a
private bill and that of a public bill. Let me read the following words:
There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked.
I ask hon. members to pay particular attention to these words:
A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy,-
Hon. members will notice the words "state policy."
-the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill,-
Hon. members will note those words.
-being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
This amendment, if allowed, would establish new legislation which would affect all bills which will hereafter be introduced into the house and would have the effect of establishing state policy. I think all hon. members, even those who have spoken to the contrary, will agree with me that this house should not establish state policy on a private bill. For the reasons which I have given, I find it necessary to rule the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Although I do not find it possible to agree with your ruling, I shall not take the time to appeal it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in connection with this bill respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. The purpose of the bill as set out in the explanatory note is to obtain authority to increase the capital stock of the company from $150,000,000 to $500,000,000. I want to join with the protests made by other hon. members in this respect.
Before passing on, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) upon the progressive stand they have taken in connection with this bill. It is an indication that opposition to the bill is not on a party basis. The principles of this bill are being opposed by more than the people of just one party because they realize that the passage of the bill in its present form is not in the public interest.
I did not expect to speak on this bill this evening, but I have been interested in the public ownership of telegraphs and telephones and I have been doing some reading in the
Bell Telephone Company

library, particularly the history of the development of the public ownership of these utilities in Europe. During my spare time in the last month I have read some four or five books dealing with the history of public ownership of telephones and telegraphs in Europe. I have been amazed to find out the sound business administration that there has been in a number of countries in Europe in the public ownership of telegraphs and telephones for over a quarter of a century in most cases and for nearly half a century in some.
Quite by chance I happened to dig up a rare book which I would suggest that the sponsor of this bill should read if he wants to be convinced of the soundness of some of our arguments. He should go to the library and get this book when we are finished.
When he is finished with the bill.

Yes. This book is entitled, "Public Ownership of Telephones on the Continent of Europe". It is one of the Harvard economic studies which was published in 1911. This is an objective survey of the public ownership of telegraphs and telephones in Europe. It is not written by people who are professed socialists or professed capitalists. I was amazed, on reading this book, to find out how far in advance of us in this country these European countries are in public ownership. I should like to read briefly from page 14 of this book as follows:
The spread of the telegraph throughout Europe was rapid once the greater countries had led the way. R. van der Borght, in his treatise "Das Verkehrswesem" gives the following dates of the opening of the various state telegraph systems to the public: 1849, Prussia and Austria; 1850, Bavaria and Saxony; 1851, Prance, Belgium, Wurtemburg, Baden; 1852, Sardinia, Parma. Modena, Tuscany, Hanover, Holland, and Switzerland; 1853, Sweden; 1854, Denmark and several of the smaller German states; 1855, Norway, Spain and Portugal;
1856,	Russia and several of the Balkan States;
1857,	the Two Sicilies; and 1859, Greece. In no country were any important lines undertaken by private enterprise. The unanimity of the contemporaneous sentiment which sanctioned the public ownership of the telegraphs was reflected in the deliberations of various parliaments and congresses.
This is an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the sentiment in favour of public ownership many years ago. Yet we in this country, operating as I think one member claimed in the debate on external affairs yesterday, under a system of progressive capitalism, have made a very modest beginning in the public ownership of

telephones and telegraphs. I continue the quotation briefly:
The policy of public ownership of telephones is now established throughout the greater part of the continent of Europe.
When was that book published?

In 1911. It goes on:
Only Spain and Denmark, among all the countries which originally declined to adopt that policy, still cling to the alternative of private ownership. The transition has only recently been completed in Italy and is still [DOT]under way in the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. In Germany, Switzerland, France, Belgium, Austria and Hungary, however, the governmental monopoly of the telephone business has been exclusive for more than a decade at the least, and in the first two of these countries for a whole generation. What are the results which have been accomplished by public enterprise in the telephone business?
Writers on the subject of public and private ownership of such business undertakings as the telephone are wont to compare the magnitudes of the business in different countries under different forms of ownership, with a view to deducing from the statistics of development under each of the two forms general conclusions in regard to their respective expediency.
The argument put forward in this objective study written by a professor of Harvard university is all in favour, from practical experience in many countries, of the public ownership of telephones.
One more quotation:
In the telephone business competition is a failure. Considered as an automatic arrangement for maintaining an accurate adjustment of the supply of telephone facilities to the demand, it easily gets out of order. So long as it remains in order its effect is to diminish the utility of the service to render which telephone facilities are created. For a while it is capable of bringing about low rates and stimulating a rapid development. Sooner or later, however, the self-interest of the competitors or the disillusionment of the public authorities will cause the termination of competition and the substitution of a regime of monopoly. This has been the result everywhere in Europe where competition has once existed, except in Stockholm, and in Stockholm the bankruptcy of the private company or the purchase of its business by the government is only a matter of time.
And so this book throughout gives definite scientific and concrete evidence in favour of the practical possibilities of the public ownership of telegraphs and telephones. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in view of the experience of other countries and in view of the nature of our development in this country, in view also of the fact that this bill would make it possible for a large monopoly to increase its capital to an exorbitant extent and would not require it to come before this parliament

Bell Telephone Company
for many years and would, in. view of the necessity that is approaching, make it very difficult and expensive to acquire control for the purpose of public ownership, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley):
That the word "now" be lefit out and the words "this day six months hence" be added at the end of the question.

speechtext: I want to make it clear that if the hon. member for Swift Current has already spoken on the motion it is not competent for him to second the amendment.
I have not spoken on the Bell Telephone bill at all, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of Bill No. 8 to grant the power asked for by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to increase its capitalization. I believe that the flow of venture capital into private and corporate enterprises should be encouraged rather than curbed at the present time. We have an increasing population, which demands increased productive facilities; also a continuing demand for many scarce goods, and capital is now plentiful and cheap.
I believe that the Bell Telephone Company has given a great service to the people of the Dominion of Canada. One could hardly realize how we could carry on business today had it not been for the invention of the telephone by Alexander Graham Bell. The Bell Telephone Company did a great job for the people of Canada during the war period. What would we have done in the way of communication had it not been for this company? In our town we have a local company that serves the local community and it is connected with the Bell Telephone Company for long distance calls. We have as fine a service as anyone could wish for.
The Bell Telephone Company is a large employer of labour and no men in any other company are used better than its employees or are more loyal. Its employees can look forward to a retirement allowance for their old age, a security that is not provided for by many companies as large as the Bell Telephone Company.
This increase of capital which the company seeks will not come out of our pockets. Anyone can buy its shares on any exchange; on the new capital issue the purchaser will be paid on his investment, and the investment will
be safe. There are many people in Canada who will look forward to getting these securities.
I do not see why there is such great opposition to this bill. The company has contributed much to the economy of our country, and I will support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have not taken half as much time on this question as either the mover of the bill or the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), who took exception to private members in the opposition expressing their opinion. It is my understanding that the private members of this house have a duty to perform. I do not think that anyone should attempt to cut them off. Incidentally it is not my intention to talk out the bill; I will stop talking long enough before nine o'clock so that hon. members will have their vote; but there is something that needs to be said, namely, in spite of the attack that the hon. member for Calgary West made upon the members of this group, and the accusations which he threw around a week ago, in the course of his speech he himself admitted that he had not thoroughly read or digested the contents of this bill. I do not think any hon. member who was not conversant with a bill under discussion should attempt to lecture any other hon. members who are attempting to clarify the principle of the bill or to express an opinion on it.
He has read hundreds of similar bills.

He should read hundreds more; it would do him a lot of good.
In his speech the hon. member for Calgary West said something very significant. There is a definite danger in these post-war years of allowing monopolies to grow to a size where they begin to threaten the public welfare. We are not alone in this opinion. Hon. members to my right who have spoken on this bill, such as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), have expressed exactly the same opinion. I believe that this house should thoroughly and carefully look into these matters in which there seems to be an attempt by half the house to push something through which has wide ramifications. Of course those of us who arc in the minority in this house cannot override the majority and will not attempt to do so. We believe in the democratic right of this parliament to take a vote on any question and we shall be content with the outcome. But there will come a time when
Bell Telephone Company

the people of this country, who are interested in the public welfare and who are interested in seeing that the public interest is safeguarded and protected, will send a majority to this house who will effectively deal with monopolies in the future.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Dauphin a question. Where did the hon. member for Calgary West say that he had not read the bill?
If I have to answer that question all I have to do is to refer the hon. member to the speech of the hon. member for Calgary West-
I have just read it over.
-in which he said that he himself had not thoroughly digested the contents of the bill.
That is quite untrue.
Just a minute. If the hon. member is going to make that statement he had better quote what the hon. member for Calgary West said.

I have no hesitation in saying that at the moment, without knowing more than has been given to us here, it seems to me too large an increase. That is said without any complete examination of the facts.
I did not use the exact words of the hon. member because I did not have the text before me. If I paraphrased his statement incorrectly andi took the wrong inference from it, of course I am sorry. There was no intention on my part to place an inaccurate construction upon his words.

speechtext:
The hour
reserved for private bills having more than expired, the house will resume the business that was interrupted at six o'clock.

Supply-External Affairs
The house resumed) consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply.

At six o'clock, Mr. Speaker,
I was speaking of the threat to world peace by the partitioning of Palestine, and I am not by any means alone in that fear. I have in my hand a copy of the New York Herald-Tribune of yesterday's date. This is a statement by the committee for justice and peace in the Holy Land:
An attempt is being made to stampede the United States government into action in a renewed effort to bring about the partitioning of .Palestine. The claim is advanced that an overwhelming majority of Americans of all faiths, support such action. We 'believe that the claim does not square with the facits; and that the attempt must be resisted . . . Many millions of American citizens are unaware of the significance of this issue in terms of our basic national interest and have not expressed themselves at all. The articulate, highly organized lobbying of those who, for a variety of partisan reasons, favour the partition of Palestine-
Mr. BLACIvMORE: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if we might not have a little order in the house. There is so much noise the hon. member has no chance to speak. It seems to me a disgrace that a condition like this should obtain.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members to be quiet while the hon. gentleman continues his remarks.

This quotation goes on:
The articulate, highly organized lobbying of those who, for a variety of partisan reasons, favour the partition of Palestine must not push us inito an action that may have the most serious consequences for our national security, our foreign policy, our friendship with the near east peoples, and the cause of world peace.
The chairman of that committee is Doctor Virginia Gildersleeve; the vice-chairmen are Doctor Henry Sloane Coffin and Rabbi Morris Lazaron. and one of the directors is Kermit Roosevelt, while numerous other distinguished Americans have signed the statement.
I should now like to say just a word about an address I heard at the united nations by Sir Carl Berendsen. Speaking about the decision last fall to partition Palestine he said:
But if there were in this room any who believed that the partition of Palestine could be accomplished peacefully and with good will on all sides and without enforcement, then I must say that that is a degree of naivete which did them little credit.
And again:
. . . those members should, on any logical basis, equally be willing to provide their proportionate share of a United States force to implement the decision to which it pledged itself last November.
I call upon my colleagues to take careful thought before they strike that tragic, perhaps irreparable blow to the united nations that would be involved in capitulation by the world to threats and violence.
I maintain that the decision to partition Palestine was itself reached under threat and by force. As Sir Carl Berendsen says, it would be impossible to carry out partition without the use of further force, or, in other words, without waging war.
In regard to the use of force in deciding upon partition, I have the statement by one of the delegates, Mrs. F. D. Roosevelt, who is reported in the New York Times of February 19 as having said that the United States government had used "legitimate" means to influence wavering delegates, thus forcing them to vote for partition. There was a curious statement I read, I think it was in an Ottawa newspaper, a quotation from the New York Times dated February 24, 1948. It said: Instead the U.N. or rather the U.S., using its enormous power, has decided to partition Palestine. In this the U.S. was powerfully aided by the Canadian delegate, about whom the following statements were made by 'the U.N. correspondent of the New York Times: "A special word should be said for Lester B. Pearson, the Canadian representative, without whose efforts it would have been impossible to imagine a decision on the Palestine question in this assembly. It was Mr. Pearson who. with untiring industry, patched up the fragile Soviet-American understanding each time the whole plan received a new blow from the British. The partition plan may turn out to be a mistake. but even a mistake is better than the deadlock which would have been inevitable had Mr. Pearson stayed in Ottawa."
I shall leave my readers to figure out that statement for themselves. I believe the Arabs have done enough. They have received into their very small country of Palestine some 600.000 Jewish refugees; and if all the other countries had done a fraction as much toward giving sanctuary to these unfortunate Jews there would certainly be no Jewish problem today. Two wrongs do not make a right. Because the Jews have been persecuted-and no one denies it-is no reason why one small country should have to bear the brunt of that wrong. May I suggest that, instead of forcing one people to bear the whole burden of this problem, the united nations should use its influence to make the world a fit place for all people, Gentile or Jew.
Supply-External Affairs

This partition means the use of force; there is no question about that. Those who favour it say it is impossible to carry out partition without force, or in other words, without starting another war. In fact the very threat of partition has started another war already. I believe, as a consequence of the methods it is pursuing, the united nations, instead of leading us to peace, is leading us nearer to world war. Instead of a world of nations united in the interests of peace, we have a world divided' into halves, each half gathering its forces against the other.
Do we want peace or do we want war? There is only one way to peace. We must stop deciding international questions at the dictation of powerful minorities, for purposes of vote catching, or for economic advantages. We all desire prosperity. Prosperity depends upon peace, and lasting peace can be secured1 only by impartial application of the principles of justice to the settlement of national and international affairs.

Mr. Speaker, unlike a good many of those who have taken part in this debate, I have not had the advantage of attending any international meetings. But after all it is the day of the common man; the common man must have his hearing, and I will speak for him tonight as well as I can.
It seems to me a good thing to have this debate. There was a time when we appeared to consider it necessary to play the ostrich and debates on foreign affairs were taboo in this house, though in saying that I am not blaming any one party. As a result of ignoring this all-important question, we came to the second war, I suppose almost worse prepared for than the first one, if that were possible. Some of us will remember that in 1914 we could hardly make ourselves believe that, after the many alarms which proved to be false, war had really come.
Well, at any rate here we are having this debate. Yesterday afternoon I had a curious feeling about it. I noticed that even on the opposite side of the house, when one would have expected that even courtesy would have kept the members in their seats to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) expounding the important matters which he did expound, the benches gradually emptied. It gave me a curious feeling about the whole thing.
None of us can doubt that when we talk about external affairs in these days we are, in very truth-in literal, actual truth-talking about matters of life and death. If anyone has any doubt about that, I would read to

him a brief quotation from Walter Lippmann, as it appeared in this morning's paper:
But if we ask ourselves why we have been discussing extra military measures since the middle of March, the answer must surely be that in the judgment of the administration there has been a change in the international situation since the events of Czechoslovakia, Finland, Berlin and Vienna. This was also the judgment of the western powers in Europe, otherwise they would not so hastily have signed the Brussels alliance. . . .
If all the governments of western Europe, of our own, have not been having an unnecessary fit of nerves, this is in truth a critical period. What will count is 'the military power which can be mobilized at once and deployed at once so that there may be a force in being. Our paramount need then is not "preparedness" for a theoretical M-day, but a mobilization of what we have and can quickly produce.
I shall have more to say about that later. I repeat that I had a curious feeling about our debate yesterday. I had the feeling that if there were any communist present-and there may well have been a communist present-he would have had rather a sense of exultation in his mind. I had the feeling he might have said to himself, "Look, these people are not really serious yet. They do not know yet the kind of world they are living in." We want the Spanish people to enjoy the blessings of freedom-freedom from dictatorships whatever their form, by whatever name they may be called.
We should face the situation as it is because, as Father Led it stated, they are trying to undermine from both ends, from the south pole and the north pole and from the middle, from the east and from the west, the strength of the British commonwealth of nations. And it will be very bad indeed if we leave the United States alone to face communist imperialism.
That is what I said when I spoke with respect to the British loan and, if my memory serves me correctly, that is what Senator Vandenberg said when he asked the senate to adopt the S3 billion loan to England from the LTnited States.
I was surprised the other day when I saw he was forgetting that Spain was holding a very strategic point, and that the United States and England should have permitted Spain to participate in the economic recovery program, due to her strategic position at the head of mare nostrum, as I call it, and to protect the interest of the western democracies from the east.

for it, because a plan was going on long before communism was in power in Russia; that is, the policy of pan-Slavism. It has been building since the congress held in Prague in the early part of the 19th century. This was the pan-Slavism of Pierre le Grand himself, who said that Russia should be going to the east as far as India. And this was taken up afterwards by Lenin who said, ''Don't worry; we are going to take the east, to keep the east; and afterwards we will deal very easily with the west."
Suppose Gibraltar were lost and the position of Spain were lost at the head of that sea. Suppose for one moment that we had lost the Italian election. Within six months we would have been at war, because there would have been pan-Slavism to take Greece and Turkey, and within one year all the middle east would have been in the hands of Soviet Russia, in the hands of communism.
When I say that, I say they are undermining the British commonwealth of nations from both ends. This is the resume I have taken from Father Ledit's story of February 9 of this year:
Feb. 10-Chili, by President Gonzales, takes possession of Graham Land in antarctic regions to south pole.
Feb. 12-Argentine sends destroyers and planes to Falkland and Maritime islands, east of Argentine. Great Britain pretends to own them since 1833.
Feb. 27-Guatemala protests against presence of British ships in waters of British Honduras and by its papers intimates that Guatemala should occupy that country (Honduras). Mexico supports this move but asks for its share of the dominion.
March 4-Salvador, Haiti, Honduras get together in support of Guatemala. Chili and Argentine sign a solidarity pact on Falkland islands.
This is undermining somewhat the feeble powers left to England or to the United Kingdom toward the south pole.
What is happening in connection with Spitzbergen? I read a speech by Ernest Dufour when he spoke to the members of the Rotary club of Hull a few days ago. He intimated in his speech that Russia had many friends in the united nations. Quoting the New York Times of January 11, 1947, he pointed out that Mr. Sulzberger, the correspondent of that paper, had said:
According to responsible diplomatic sources, the Norwegian government proposed to the Soviet union on April 9, 1945, the joint defence of Spitsbergen. The offer is said to have been made while Trygve Lie was Foreign Minister of Norway.
Then, in the Toronto Star of June 10, 1947, we find the following by Ross Munro:
The Spitzbergen question, involving Russia's desire to establish a military base on the

mountainous archipelago 650 miles [DOT] from the north pole is the number one international headache for Norway, which has sovereignty over the islands.
It was in 1945, and while Trygve Lie was Minister for Norway, that they were ready to give to Russia the same participation in Spitzbergen as they had themselves. There was a treaty, I believe, signed by Canada. Canada was interested in it, states Ross Munro, not only because the island was on the direct air route between the main cities of northern Russia, Canada and the United States, but also because she signed a treaty in 1920 which gave Norway sovereignty over the archipelago never to be used for military purposes.
They are undermining the British commonwealth of nations from both ends. I do not wish to create friction against any country, but now that we know that there is an undermining of the strength of the third imperialism, we have to stand on our own feet with United States imperialism and we should build a triangle composed of Greenland, Iceland and Newfoundland in which to erect naval and air bases to protect the Arctic area against invasion should we lose Europe to communism. This is in support of what I said last year. I did not want to refer to a previous debate, but hon. members will remember that Bill 238 granted certain privileges to the United States army on Canadian territory. I remember my hon. friends over there were against it because they contended that we were granting privileges to United States soldiers. I said, as reported on page 3926 of Hansard:
As I understand the bill, we are trying to be co-defendants after having been co-belligerents. When you hear a member from Quebec speaking in favour of an accord with the United States, or in favour of privileges to be given the United States army, it is not because we in Quebec want to turn our eyes away from the British empire or the British commonwealth of nations and turn them toward the United States of America for good, leaving the former alone. It is just because we have the experience of the last war, because we want those two organizations, those two nations or groups of nations, to stand firmly on their feet right in front of the menace from without and from within.
I took the same stand in making my point tonight in favour of Spain. I want these two groups of nations to stand firmly on their feet and face the real menace which at last everyone seems to understand. I was somewhat apprehensive when I got up to speak tonight; but I became quite satisfied during this debate when I saw that at last everyone in this house, and perhaps everyone in the western democracies, realize the peril which we have been pointing out for ten years and which will always be here. I am glad that

Let us live our Christian lives thoroughly and carry out Christian principles in the international field. We do not need to worry, because victory is ahead; it is just up to us to take it.

Mr. Speaker, this debate on foreign relations has been very sane and on a good basis and I hope it remains that way. Foreign relations now dominate the thinking and actions of all domestic political forces more than ever before. The same may be said about foreign relations dominating the thinking and actions of domestic economic forces whether they like it or not. I should like to give an example of this by quoting from page 2418 of Hansard of March 19, 1948. At that time the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell) asked the following question, which was answered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe):
I want to ask the minister one simple question. I am much impressed, as I hear him talk, as to the position of the milling and other industries. He says that the government will do this and the government will do that, and that as long as these people will do what they are told, they will be well off. Perhaps they will. Would I be wrong in calling this a highly socialistic measure ?
Mr. Howe: State marketing is socialism, yes, if you like. But it is hard to be different in a world that at the moment is following state marketing for reasons which I think are largely beyond their control. There are currency problems, credit problems and a number of factors, which are driving countries to state marketing at the present time.
I should like to point out that the basis of our economy in the final analysis reflects itself in definite political form at home and affects our outlook abroad. For example, if this country were sold on state marketing within as well as state marketing without we would be expressing ourselves in a form of barter arrangements externally rather than following such international legislation as the Geneva trade pacts, which agreements are attempting to reimpose international laissez faire.
With a changing world facing us, our problem at home is to maintain democracy and extend it in the face of that change. There are two extremes fighting for control in the world at the present time over this ever-increasing state apparatus. Whether one considers himself a Liberal or a Conservative, it must be recognized that the state is playing an ever-increasing role in the economic life of the country. Fascism and communism are the two extremes. The best recent example of fascism in the world today is the growth of de Gaullism in France, which of course is being opposed by communism under Thorez. Both are driving each other to further excesses. They are both fighting on the decrepit and tattered remains of laissez faire.
If this statement does not meet with your approval, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote an extremely respectable source, Don Cameron in the Windsor Star. He is the columnist who perhaps has led the field in the anti-communist drive in Canada. In the Windsor Star of March 20, under "Answer No. 6", he writes:
There is no cure for communism because communism is not a disease, it is a symptom. It is the expression of the vast unrest that permeates all the people of the world, not excepting our own, as the result of the moral, spiritual and economic breakdowns of "bourgeois capitalism."
It has been lucky for capitalism that there has been a corresponding moral breakdown in the communist party, if one deals with the ' communist party as a political expression of the working class.
I should like to bring to mind Lenin's slogan at the time of the Russian revolution, "No annexations and no reparations". Russia today is leading the field in annexations and reparations. One thing that can be said about the old socialist philosophy is that it never believed in blaming the workers of any country for the war. They blamed the masters. But an entirely different attitude is taken by Russia at the present time.
I should like to quote, and add to in support of my argument, from "Left-Wing Communism -an Infantile Disorder", by V. I. Lenin:
